title: 2 Kings 10:18–31
context: Jehu announces that he will serve Baal more than Ahab did and summons all Baal’s prophets, worshipers, and priests to a great sacrifice, acting deceptively in order to destroy them. With the temple of Baal full, and after making sure no servants of the LORD are present, he has his guards kill the worshipers. The temple’s pillars are burned and the building torn down. The narrator states that Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel, yet did not turn from Jeroboam’s golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The LORD commends Jehu for carrying out judgment on Ahab’s house and promises his descendants the throne to the fourth generation, but the text adds that Jehu did not walk in the LORD’s law with all his heart.

verses.text: Jehu gathered all the people together, and said to them, “Ahab served Baal a little, but Jehu will serve him much.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu tells the people that Ahab served Baal a little, but he will serve Baal much. Arminian readers note that this is deliberate deception, as the next verse makes clear, used to gather all of Baal’s worshipers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the deception as Jehu’s own strategy, which the narrator reports without commending it. Shared ground: both traditions read the speech as a ruse rather than a sincere statement of devotion to Baal.

verses.text: Now therefore call to me all the prophets of Baal, all of his worshipers, and all of his priests. Let no one be absent, for I have a great sacrifice to Baal. Whoever is absent, he shall not live.” But Jehu did deceptively, intending to destroy the worshipers of Baal.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu summons all Baal’s prophets, worshipers, and priests, acting deceptively to destroy them. Arminian readers note that the narrator openly calls his act deceptive, giving readers the moral information they need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Jehu’s aim of removing Baal worship as consistent with the covenant, while his method is reported plainly as deceit. Both traditions read the verse with attention to both the goal and the means.

verses.text: Jehu said, “Sanctify a solemn assembly for Baal!” So they proclaimed it.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu orders a solemn assembly for Baal, and it is proclaimed. Arminian readers note the irony of using the language of sacred assembly to set a trap for those who worship a false god.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as exposing the extent of Baal worship in Israel. Shared ground: the verse continues the account of Jehu’s ruse, reported as narrative without approval of the deception.

verses.text: Jehu sent through all Israel; and all the worshipers of Baal came, so that there was not a man left that didn’t come. They came into the house of Baal; and the house of Baal was filled from one end to another.
verses.arminianNotes: All of Baal’s worshipers come, filling the house of Baal from end to end. Arminian readers note the large number of worshipers, showing how deeply Baal worship had taken root under Ahab’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the full temple as revealing the scale of Israel’s apostasy. Both traditions read the verse as setting the scene for the destruction of Baal worship, reported in the following verses.

verses.text: He said to him who kept the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for all the worshipers of Baal!” So he brought robes out to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu has robes brought out for all of Baal’s worshipers. Arminian readers note the practical detail, which may have helped distinguish the worshipers from others present, though the text does not explain it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the robes as part of the ritual that Jehu uses to identify those he intends to destroy. Shared ground: the verse is a brief detail of the ruse, whose exact purpose is not stated in the text.

verses.text: Jehu went with Jehonadab the son of Rechab into the house of Baal. Then he said to the worshipers of Baal, “Search, and see that none of the servants of the LORD are here with you, but only the worshipers of Baal.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu and Jehonadab enter the house of Baal, and Jehu orders that no servants of the LORD be present. Arminian readers note the concern to protect worshipers of the LORD from what is about to happen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the separation as drawing a clear line between the servants of the LORD and those of Baal. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the coming judgment is aimed specifically at Baal worship.

verses.text: So they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Now Jehu had appointed for himself eighty men outside, and said, “If any of the men whom I bring into your hands escape, he who lets him go, his life shall be for the life of him.”
verses.arminianNotes: The worshipers offer sacrifices, while Jehu stations eighty men outside with orders that none escape. Arminian readers note the careful planning and the threat of death for any guard who lets a worshiper go.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as moving toward the end of Baal worship in Israel. Shared ground: the verse reports the preparation soberly, as the narrative does, without dwelling on the violence to come.

verses.text: As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, Jehu said to the guard and to the captains, “Go in and kill them! Let no one escape.” So they struck them with the edge of the sword. The guard and the captains threw the bodies out, and went to the inner shrine of the house of Baal.
verses.arminianNotes: When the offering is finished, Jehu orders the guards to kill the worshipers, and they do. Arminian readers state the event plainly as the text gives it, without elaboration or endorsement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the act within the covenant’s judgment on idolatry in Israel, while recognizing that this was a specific event in Israel’s history. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as narrative, never as a pattern for today.

verses.text: They brought out the pillars that were in the house of Baal and burned them.
verses.arminianNotes: The pillars in the house of Baal are brought out and burned. Arminian readers note the destruction of the objects of false worship, removing them from Israel’s religious life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the burning of the pillars as fulfilling the law’s command to destroy idolatrous objects (compare Deuteronomy 7:5). Both traditions read the verse as part of Jehu’s removal of Baal worship from Israel.

verses.text: They broke down the pillar of Baal, and broke down the house of Baal, and made it a latrine, to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: They break down the pillar and house of Baal and make it a latrine to this day. Arminian readers note the deliberate defilement of the site, ensuring that it could never again be used for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the act as a decisive and lasting rejection of Baal worship. Shared ground: the phrase “to this day” reflects the narrator’s perspective, and both traditions read the verse as marking the end of the temple.

verses.text: Thus Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel. Arminian readers see a real and significant achievement, the removal of a false worship that had brought Israel to the brink of abandoning the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using Jehu to accomplish His purpose of removing Baal worship. Both traditions read the verse as the narrator’s summary of what Jehu achieved, before turning to what he failed to do.

verses.text: However, Jehu didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin—the golden calves that were in Bethel and that were in Dan.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu did not turn from Jeroboam’s sins, the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Arminian readers note that his reform was incomplete, removing Baal while keeping the calf worship begun by Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28–30).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a sobering qualification of Jehu’s zeal. Shared ground: both traditions read the narrator’s verdict as showing that zeal against one false worship does not guarantee faithful obedience in all things.

verses.text: The LORD said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in executing that which is right in my eyes, and have done to Ahab’s house according to all that was in my heart, your descendants shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commends Jehu for doing what was right in His eyes against Ahab’s house and promises his line the throne to the fourth generation. Arminian readers see God honoring a specific act of obedience (compare 15:12).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s commendation as tied to the task He appointed, not as a judgment on Jehu’s whole heart. Both traditions read the promise alongside 10:31; on how God uses flawed agents, see the existing contrasts at Judges 9:23 and Isaiah 10:7.

verses.text: But Jehu took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He didn’t depart from the sins of Jeroboam, with which he made Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehu took no heed to walk in the LORD’s law with all his heart and kept Jeroboam’s sins. Arminian readers see a real failure of response, showing that outward zeal can coexist with a divided heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as revealing that Jehu’s obedience was partial and his heart not wholly given to God. Shared ground: both traditions read 10:30–31 together, with Hosea 1:4 as a hedged cross-reference that later prophecy also evaluated his house.
